newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Rescuers race weather to find ski resort survivors.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers race weather to find ski resort survivors.

text.p: Rescuers on Monday raced against the weather to find 10 people still entombed in the rubble of an Australian ski resort, hoping for a repeat of one man's miracle survival.

Another perfect, cloudless day dawned on Thredbo on Monday, but rescuers were working feverishly to prepare for wet weather, fearing a downpour could send the tonnes of concrete slabs, twisted metal, dirt and trees crashing further down the hill.
"We are planning for rain," police superintendent Charlie Sanderson told reporters.
"All the experts tell us that it could rain on Wednesday and it will almost certainly rain and snow on Thursday," he said.

Stuart Diver, a fit 27-year-old ski instructor, stunned the world on Saturday night when he emerged from his concrete sarcophagus deep within the debris at the Thredbo resort, southwest of Sydney, after surviving for three freezing nights.

"Stuart has been released from intensive care and he is back in the (general) wards of Canberra Hospital," ambulance service spokesman Bill Williams told reporters at Thredbo, about 150 km (90 miles) south of Canberra.
"He is very positive and he has had a very speedy recovery."

A total of 20 people were buried late on Wednesday night when a heavily populated, steep hillside gave way, sending one ski lodge crashing into another below it. So far, nine bodies have been recovered from the unstable wreckage.
Rescuers have honeycombed the debris with 24 metres (80 feet) of tunnels, burrowing by hand if need be to look for cavities that might hide life.
"One must hope that there are (more survivors) but obviously as time goes on, it's getting more and more difficult," fire brigade superintendent Ray Kelly told reporters.
Tunnelling was suspended overnight on Sunday, as rescuers switched to preparing the slope for rain.
They cleared dirt from the top of the landslide and arranged for tarpaulins to be draped over a 40 metre (130 feet) by 80 metre (260 feet) patch of unstable dirt.
A big concrete slab will later be hoisted from the debris, Sanderson said. "That slab will be removed and that will give us much better access to what's below," he added.

Family and friends of the landslide victims will gather on Monday afternoon with dignitaries, including acting prime minister Tim Fischer, at Thredbo's modern granite and timber chapel to pray for more survivors and to reflect on the tragedy.
The small community, with a permanent population of barely 500, has been numbed by the disaster, which has touched all of them. They find the big media presence especially uncomfortable.
Newspapers around the world on Monday carried the remarkable story of Diver's survival after being sandwiched between concrete slabs for 64 hours and at one point almost drowning in groundwater.

Diver and his wife Sally, who is still missing, were in bed when the disaster struck. Diver has told rescuers how he pressed his nose against the concrete slab above his head in order to breath as water and mud filled his concrete tomb.
Some rescuers have said Diver tried desperately to save his wife after the landslide hit, but her fate is still unclear.
Police have not identified any of the nine bodies that have been recovered so far. In some cases, victims' teeth will need to be examined before they can be identified, police said.
In warmer climates, victims of building collapses have survived for over a week, especially if water is present.

In South Korea last year, a woman trapped with food and water survived for 16 days in a collapsed department store. In 1990, a woman was pulled alive from debris 13 days after one of China's worst recorded earthquakes.
